exam: A 30‑year‑old with a history of rheumatic fever presents with exertional dyspnoea; what bedside findings differentiate mitral stenosis from regurgitation? — Identify opening snap and diastolic rumble for stenosis; holosystolic murmur radiating to axilla for regurgitation.

A patient in a rural clinic has sudden pulmonary oedema; what is the immediate management and why is valve intervention delayed? — Give high‑flow oxygen and IV furosemide; stabilise before arranging transfer for possible balloon commissurotomy.
How does atrial fibrillation alter the clinical picture of mitral valve disease? — Loss of atrial kick reduces ventricular filling, worsening symptoms; rate control is essential.
Why is penicillin prophylaxis recommended lifelong in rheumatic mitral disease? — Prevents recurrent streptococcal infections that can cause further valve damage.

When is balloon mitral commissurotomy indicated over surgical replacement? — In severe stenosis with valve area ≤1.5 cm², pliable leaflets, and no significant regurgitation, especially when surgical resources are limited.

What laboratory or imaging result might falsely suggest mild disease in a patient with severe mitral regurgitation? — Normal chest X‑ray may miss severe regurgitation; rely on echo or POCUS for accurate grading.

Explain why diuretics are used in mitral regurgitation but can worsen forward output in severe stenosis. — Diuretics reduce pulmonary congestion in regurgitation but may lower preload needed to cross a narrowed mitral orifice in stenosis.

What are the contraindications to using ACE inhibitors in mitral valve disease? — Not contraindicated; however, caution in severe aortic stenosis or renal failure; they are used for afterload reduction in regurgitation.
ai.title: Mitral Valve Disease
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Mitral valve disease includes stenosis and regurgitation that impair left‑heart filling or output. In low‑resource settings rheumatic fever remains the common cause, but other infections and systemic illnesses also contribute.

b: Murmur characteristics differentiate stenosis vs regurgitation
Atrial fibrillation often accompanies chronic disease
sections.p: Abnormal structure or function of the mitral valve causing obstruction (stenosis) or leakage (regurgitation). Diagnosis relies on clinical signs and bedside echocardiography when available.

b: Mitral valve area ≤1.5 cm² = severe stenosis
Effective regurgitant orifice ≥0.4 cm² = severe regurgitation
sections.p: Severity is graded by valve area (stenosis) or regurgitant volume (regurgitation) and by symptoms (NYHA class).

b: Rheumatic fever – most common, especially in children with repeated streptococcal infections
Infective endocarditis – often from poor dental hygiene or IV drug use
Systemic lupus erythematosus – immune complex deposition
Congenital mitral valve prolapse – rare but possible
sections.p: In East Africa the leading cause is rheumatic heart disease; other contributors include infective endocarditis, lupus, and congenital malformations.

b: Loud opening snap + diastolic rumble → stenosis
Holosystolic high‑pitched murmur at apex radiating to axilla → regurgitation
Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic early. Progressive dyspnoea, orthopnoea, palpitations, and fatigue are typical; acute severe regurgitation can cause pulmonary oedema.
Use bedside tools first; refer for echocardiography when possible.

t.b: Is the murmur systolic or diastolic? → Determines stenosis vs regurgitation
Shows atrial enlargement or fibrillation → Indicates chronic pressure overload
Shows left atrial enlargement or pulmonary congestion → Supports severity assessment
Measures valve area, regurgitant volume, and pulmonary pressures → Provides definitive grading
Detects gross valve thickening and regurgitant jet when echo machine unavailable → Guides urgent decisions

b: Acute pulmonary oedema – requires immediate oxygen and diuretics
Atrial thrombus → systemic emboli, stroke
Right‑heart failure from chronic pulmonary hypertension
sections.p: Complications arise from pressure overload, volume overload, or embolic phenomena.

b: Penicillin prophylaxis for rheumatic fever to prevent progression
Furosemide for pulmonary congestion – avoids fluid overload
Beta‑blockers or digoxin for rate control in atrial fibrillation
Refer for percutaneous balloon commissurotomy (stenosis) or surgical repair/replacement (regurgitation) when severe
sections.p: Treat underlying cause, control symptoms, and refer for valve intervention when indicated.

b: Educate on prompt treatment of streptococcal throat infections
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce respiratory decompensation
sections.p: Regular clinical review every 6–12 months; echo every 1–2 years in stable disease. Primary prevention of rheumatic fever is essential.
